metaData.originalTitle: It’s the biggest World Cup but is the gap between best and worst teams smaller than ever?
metaData.title: It’s the biggest World Cup but is the gap between best and worst teams smaller than ever?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article examines whether the gap between top and bottom teams has narrowed in the expanded 2026 World Cup, using data to show that while average winning margins are higher, minnows have produced resilient draws, though upsets are mostly draws rather than wins.
metaData.summary: The article analyzes the competitive balance of the 2026 World Cup after its expansion to 48 teams. It presents data showing the tournament has the lowest average FIFA ranking (32.4) on record and a higher average winning margin (2.3 goals) than previous group stages. However, the author argues that these surface-level statistics mask compelling underdog stories, such as Cape Verde holding Spain and Uruguay to draws, and Curacao drawing with Ecuador after a heavy loss. The analysis uses historical comparisons to show that underdogs have always been competitive in World Cups, avoiding defeat roughly once every three encounters. While the expanded format creates more ranking mismatches, the rate of upset wins has not dramatically increased; most surprises are draws. The article concludes that fears of minnows being overwhelmed have proved unfounded, and the class of 2026 continues a tradition of spirited resistance.

mainPoints.point: Expanded World Cup increases average winning margin and low average ranking, but that doesn't capture underdog stories.
mainPoints.explanation: The tournament has a 2.3 goal average winning margin and average team ranking of 32.4, suggesting a diluted field, but standout performances like Cape Verde's draws show resilience.

mainPoints.point: Upsets are mostly draws rather than wins; historical underdog win rate hasn't risen significantly.
mainPoints.explanation: Most ranking mismatches end in draws for lower-ranked teams, with only two wins by teams ranked 30+ places below opponents (Ghana and South Africa), consistent with historical patterns.

mainPoints.point: More ranking mismatches occur due to expansion, but underdog performance rate remains similar.
mainPoints.explanation: There have been eight matches with ranking gap >50 in this tournament alone (previously six total from 1994-2022), yet lower-ranked teams avoid defeat in about 50% of severe mismatches, similar to past tournaments.

mainPoints.point: Historical comparison shows minnows have always been capable of battling against the odds.
mainPoints.explanation: The article compares to 2002 World Cup where Senegal and South Korea earned wins that sparked deep runs, but overall underdog success rates are consistent across eras.

keyQuotes: History shows that World Cup minnows have always been capable of battling admirably against the odds, and the class of 2026 is no exception.
Fears that they would be swallowed up by the established favourites, though, have proved well wide of the mark.
